title: Shopping, colors and pointing words
goal: Shop from start to checkout, name colors and sizes, and use **three levels of pointing words** — where English has only two.
bekal: naming colors and sizes with the matching endings
asking for discounts and paying with phrases people really use

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Numa loja de roupas
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a shirt for a classmate's birthday party.

lines.text: Oi! Posso ajudar ou só está olhando?

notes: ⚠️ **Em quantas vezes? is the question that puzzles foreigners most in Brazil.** Literally "in how many times?", it asks how many monthly **installments** you want to split the purchase into. In Brazil, paying for a fifteen-dollar item in three interest-free installments is perfectly normal. The right answer if you want to pay in one go: *À vista* ("in full").

**Estou procurando** — the "-ing" form, covered fully in unit 19. For now just recognize the pattern: *estar* + a verb ending in **-ndo**, just like English "I am looking". Brazilians use it constantly; in Portugal people say *estou a procurar*.
**Sai por** literally "goes out for", means "comes to". It's a casual way to state a price in a shop: *Sai por cem reais*. Its sibling *fica por* means the same.

**Essa aqui, aquela ali** — notice how pointing words always pair up with a place word. Brazilians hardly ever say *esse* without *aqui*, or *aquele* without *ali*. That pairing makes the meaning clear without having to point.
**Linda** is stronger than *bonita*. Roughly: *bonito* (nice) → *lindo* (gorgeous) → *maravilhoso* (amazing). Brazilians hand out all three generously.

grammars.title: Three levels of pointing words
body: English has two: "this" and "that". Portuguese has three, and the third marks something far from **both** speakers.
after: **In Brazil, este and esse have merged in practice.** Grammar books separate *este* (near me) from *esse* (near you), but Brazilians use **esse** for both, in speech and in casual writing. If you use *esse* for everything nearby and *aquele* for things far away, you already sound Brazilian.

**The neutral forms (isso, aquilo) are used when the thing isn't named**: *O que é isso?* ("What's this?"), *Isso é caro* ("That's expensive"). As soon as the noun appears, you go back to the masculine or feminine form: *esse livro*, *essa camisa*.
⚠️ Pointing words also fuse with prepositions: *de + esse* = **desse**, *em + esse* = **nesse**, *de + aquele* = **daquele**. The pattern is the same as *do* and *no* from unit 8.

grammars.title: Colors
body: Ordinary adjectives, so their endings match the noun. Those ending in *-e* or a consonant don't change for gender.
after: The three rows that **never change** — *cinza*, *rosa*, *laranja* — have a nice reason: they're really names of things (ash, rose, orange), and names of things don't adapt. *Uma camisa rosa*, *dois carros laranja*.
Colors go **after** the noun, like all adjectives: *a camisa azul*, *o carro vermelho* — the reverse of English "the blue shirt".

grammars.title: Shopping phrases
body: Ten phrases that cover almost every transaction.
after: **Demais means "too"** and goes after its adjective: *caro demais* (too expensive), *pequeno demais* (too small). It's also used on its own as praise: *Legal demais!* = "so cool!"
*Tem desconto?* is fine to ask at markets and small shops, but not in malls or supermarkets. If you pay cash, your chances are much better — try adding *à vista*.

blocks.text: *O chinelo* — flip-flops — deserves a mention of its own because it's so much a part of everyday Brazilian life that people wear them to the supermarket, the beach, and sometimes the office. The best-known brand, Havaianas, has become a household word.

**Pix has been the most common way to pay in Brazil since 2020** — an instant, free bank transfer accepted everywhere from big malls to coconut sellers on the beach. If you stay in Brazil for more than a month, you'll use it more often than cash.
*Tem troco para cinquenta?* = "Do you have change for fifty?" — a handy question, because small vendors in Brazil often run out of small bills.

items: What are you doing tomorrow? → *O que você vai fazer amanhã?*
I'm going to stay home → *Eu vou ficar em casa*
We're going to travel in July → *Nós vamos viajar em julho*
You're going to love it → *Você vai adorar*
How about a coffee? → *Que tal um café?*
